overview: Gerdau S.A. is Brazil's largest steel producer and the largest producer of long steel in the Americas, operating an integrated and mini-mill network across Brazil, North America (U.S./Canada), South America (Argentina, Peru, Uruguay, plus JV interests in Colombia/Dominican Republic) and a Special Steel division (Brazil and U.S.). The company also owns iron ore mining assets in Minas Gerais, Brazil, which feed its integrated Ouro Branco mill, providing a degree of raw-material self-sufficiency. Gerdau reports in Brazilian Reais (IFRS) and trades on the NYSE as an ADR (GGB, preferred shares) and on B3 (GGBR3/GGBR4).

business_model.summary: Gerdau converts steel scrap (mini-mill/electric arc furnace route) and, in Brazil, iron ore/pig iron (integrated blast-furnace route at Ouro Branco) into long steel products (rebar, merchant bar, wire rod, structural shapes) and, to a lesser extent, flat and special steel products, sold mostly to construction, manufacturing, automotive and energy/infrastructure end markets. Revenue is overwhelmingly transactional/commodity in nature (volume x steel spread), not recurring, and highly sensitive to regional steel prices, scrap costs and capacity utilization. North America has become the key profit engine post-2025 U.S. tariff increases, generating the majority of consolidated EBITDA despite being a smaller share of revenue.

revenue_streams.name: Brazil Business Division (BD)
revenue_streams.trend: pressured by record steel imports, soft construction/manufacturing demand

revenue_streams.name: North America BD
revenue_streams.trend: growing - ~62% of 2025 consolidated EBITDA, benefiting from Section 232 tariffs and data center/infrastructure demand

revenue_streams.name: South America BD (ex-Brazil)
revenue_streams.trend: stable/small, exposed to Argentina/Peru macro cycles

revenue_streams.name: Special Steel BD (Brazil + U.S.)
revenue_streams.trend: cyclical, tied to automotive/industrial demand, recent price increases

revenue_streams.name: Iron ore / mining
revenue_streams.trend: growing - Miguel Burnier expansion ramping in 2026, targeted ~BRL 1.1bn incremental annual EBITDA at full ramp

business_model.customer_type: B2B - construction companies, steel distributors/service centers, fabricators, OEMs (automotive, agricultural and industrial equipment), and increasingly data center/renewable energy/transmission infrastructure customers in North America
business_model.geographic_mix: Brazil (largest revenue base, historically largest EBITDA contributor, now overtaken by North America on profitability), North America (U.S./Canada - highest-ever share of consolidated EBITDA, ~62% in 2025), South America ex-Brazil (Argentina, Peru, Uruguay, JV stakes in Colombia/Dominican Republic), Special Steel (Brazil + U.S.)

main_competitors: Chinese steel exporters (structural competitive pressure via imports)
competitive_position.market_position: Largest crude steel producer in Brazil and largest long-steel producer in the Americas; #2 long-steel producer in North America by volume (via the former Gerdau Ameristeel platform). No single competitor matches Gerdau's full product breadth in Brazil, but it faces fragmented, intense regional competition everywhere it operates.

moat_factors.description: Rebar/merchant bar economics are regional (freight-cost driven, ~350-500 mile radius); Gerdau's geographically dispersed mills near raw materials, ports and customers provide a durable regional cost/logistics advantage.

Gerdau owns iron ore mines in Minas Gerais feeding the integrated Ouro Branco mill, partially insulating Brazilian integrated production from seaborne ore price swings; being expanded via the Miguel Burnier project.

U.S. Section 232 tariffs (50% on most imports since mid-2025) and Brazil's tariff-rate quotas (25% above-quota tariff on 19 product categories through June 2027) plus anti-dumping duties on Chinese flat products create meaningful, policy-dependent protection in Gerdau's two largest markets.
Widest long-steel product range in Brazil and a diversified North American/Special Steel portfolio lets Gerdau serve large, multi-product customers that smaller regional mills cannot.
Century-old family-controlled brand with long-standing distributor and OEM relationships, but limited pricing power given commodity product nature.

weaknesses: Commodity product with minimal differentiation and essentially no switching costs for customers - price is the primary competitive factor
Brazilian operations structurally exposed to a domestic industry running near ~35% of installed national capacity amid a surge in low-cost (often Chinese-origin) imports

Moat is largely a function of government trade policy (Section 232, Brazilian TRQs) rather than intrinsic structural advantage - durability is uncertain beyond stated tariff sunset dates (Brazil's TRQ renewed through June 2027; USMCA review ongoing)
No long-term contracted/recurring revenue; essentially full exposure to steel-price and volume cyclicality

growth_drivers: U.S. Section 232 tariffs (50% on most steel imports since June 2025) rebalancing domestic supply/demand and lifting North American capacity utilization, shipments and prices
North American demand pull from data centers, renewable energy, transmission infrastructure and semiconductor plant construction
Miguel Burnier iron ore mining expansion (ramping through 2026) and other Brazilian mining projects targeted to add ~BRL 1.4-1.5bn in combined annual EBITDA at full ramp
Texas (Midlothian) EAF capacity expansion (+150,000 tons/year from 2026) to capture U.S. tariff-protected demand
Brazilian tariff-rate quotas and anti-dumping duties (through at least June 2027) shielding domestic long-steel pricing from the worst of Chinese import competition
Decarbonization/low-carbon product line (NewEco) and renewable self-generation (Barro Alto solar complex, ~13% of Brazilian electricity needs) supporting cost and ESG positioning
Ongoing portfolio optimization - restructuring low-return Brazilian assets (e.g., Açonorte/Recife) while reallocating capital toward higher-return North American and mining projects
Active capital return program: 2026 share buyback (up to ~4.4% of preferred shares and ~10% of common shares, 31% complete as of Q2 2026) plus minimum 30% payout dividend policy

business.risk: Brazilian steel imports at record levels
business.description: Import penetration into Latin America hit a record ~40% in 2025/2026 with China supplying ~45% of those imports; even with tariff-rate quotas, Brazilian operations continue to see margin pressure and have required asset restructuring (e.g., Recife).

Revenue and margins are highly sensitive to global/regional steel spreads, construction and auto-sector demand, and capacity utilization; the industry structurally has excess global supply (led by China).
Heavy reliance on construction and manufacturing/automotive demand, both of which are credit- and rate-sensitive, particularly in Brazil.
Gerdau has had to reassess a planned ~$500 million special-steel plant in Mexico due to U.S. tariffs reducing the economics of exporting Mexican-made steel to the U.S.

Gerdau operates tailings dams in Minas Gerais (relevant given Brazil's history of catastrophic dam failures at other mining companies); any structural failure would carry severe reputational, legal and operational consequences.

financial.description: Financial statements are in BRL while a significant share of debt, and increasingly earnings, are USD-linked (North America); BRL volatility against the USD creates translation and transaction risk, and historically has driven large swings in reported results.

Gerdau carries large, long-running Brazilian tax disputes (ICMS, goodwill amortization deductibility, income tax on foreign profits) worth billions of reais, some unreserved, with uncertain timing and outcome.

Net debt/EBITDA is currently low (~0.69x as of Q2 2026) and the balance sheet is intentionally conservative, but historically credit-rating downgrades (Moody's 2016) have raised financing costs; sovereign rating actions on Brazil remain a pass-through risk.

regulatory.risk: U.S. Section 232 tariff reversal or USMCA renegotiation
regulatory.description: Gerdau's North American profitability is now heavily dependent on the 50% Section 232 tariffs; any reduction, carve-outs, or adverse outcome in ongoing USMCA review talks could quickly erode the North American margin advantage that now drives the majority of group EBITDA.

Brazil's tariff-rate quota regime (25% above-quota tariff on 19 product categories) is set through June 2027 and anti-dumping duties on Chinese flat products are time-limited (five-year renewable); non-renewal or watering-down would reopen the domestic market to cheaper imports.
Stricter tailings-dam and environmental licensing rules following industry-wide dam failures in Brazil increase compliance costs and could delay mining expansion projects like Miguel Burnier.

macro.risk: China's excess steel capacity and export intensity
macro.description: Persistent overcapacity in China continues to generate elevated steel exports into Latin America and globally, structurally pressuring prices and import penetration outside of tariff-protected markets.

macro.risk: Brazilian interest rates and GDP growth
macro.description: High Selic rates have suppressed Brazilian construction activity; rate cuts (Selic forecast ~13.5% for 2026, down from peaks) should eventually help demand, but transmission to construction activity takes several quarters.
As a cyclical commodity producer, Gerdau's earnings are highly levered to global industrial production, construction cycles and infrastructure spending.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global steel markets remain oversupplied, led by Chinese production/export intensity, while the U.S. market has been reset more favorably for domestic producers by the 2025 Section 232 tariff increase to 50%. Brazil's domestic steel industry is running at roughly 35% of installed capacity amid record import penetration, even with tariff-rate quotas in place; recovery is tied to further Selic rate cuts feeding through to construction activity.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - steel is a classically cyclical commodity business tied to construction, manufacturing and automotive end-demand, with volatile spreads between steel prices and scrap/ore input costs.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High and bidirectional - Brazilian Selic rate cuts should eventually boost domestic construction/steel demand (with a multi-quarter lag), while U.S./global rate levels affect broader industrial activity and data-center/infrastructure capex that is currently supporting North American volumes.
key_input_costs: Iron ore and pig iron (Brazil integrated route)
Electricity/energy (rising Brazilian energy costs cited as a 2026 headwind)
Freight/logistics (North American freight costs rose ~8.5% QoQ in Q2 2026 on fuel inflation)

recent_developments.event: Consolidated adjusted EBITDA of ~BRL 3.4bn, the highest since Q3 2023; adjusted net income up 45% sequentially to BRL 1.5bn; North American shipments +7% YoY and adjusted EBITDA +15% QoQ on data center, renewable energy and infrastructure demand; Brazil showed only modest improvement amid elevated import penetration.
Profit jumped ~34% YoY with North America delivering ~75% of EBITDA growth, as post-tariff U.S. pricing and volumes continued to outperform a still-weak Brazilian market.

Board approved a new 18-month share buyback program (up to 55,000,000 preferred shares, ~4.4% of preferred, and up to 1,441,120 common shares, ~10% of common) and approved cancellation of shares already held in treasury (418,800 common / 7,700,000 preferred).

FY2025 results showed North America ending the year with its highest-ever share of consolidated EBITDA (~62%), while Brazil posted a 'flat' Q4 profit as U.S. strength offset domestic weakness; Gerdau filed its FY2025 20-F with the SEC and CVM.

Gerdau restructured its Açonorte unit in Recife, halting steelmaking/rolling and focusing on drawn products (wire, mesh, nails), eliminating ~160 positions, as part of a broader reshaping of its North American and Brazilian footprint in response to tariffs and import pressure.

U.S. Section 232 tariffs increased from 25% (effective March 2025, covering Canada, Mexico, EU, Japan, South Korea, UK, Argentina, Australia, Brazil and others) to 50% in June 2025 (UK remained at 25% pending negotiations), materially boosting Gerdau's North American capacity utilization and realized prices.
Gerdau confirmed it was reassessing a planned ~US$500 million special-steel plant investment in Mexico given reduced economics of exporting Mexican-made steel to the U.S. under the new tariff regime.

Brazil renewed its tariff-rate quota regime (25% tariff on above-quota imports across 19 product categories) through June 2027, alongside existing five-year anti-dumping duties on Chinese cold-rolled, hot-dip galvanized and pre-painted flat steel; regional import penetration nonetheless hit a record ~40% in 2025/2026, with China supplying ~45% of Latin American imports.
Board approved a dividend of R$0.23 per share (~R$451.3 million total), consistent with the policy of distributing a minimum 30% of parent-company net income.

items.notes: Recent price increases in special steels and beams not yet fully reflected in guidance, implying potential upside; freight cost inflation (~8.5% QoQ) is a partial offset.
Management signaled savings would be redirected toward competitiveness/growth investments rather than balance-sheet repair, given net debt/EBITDA already low (~0.69x).

guidance.management_commentary: Management struck a cautiously optimistic tone on North America, citing resilient demand from data centers, renewable energy and infrastructure, while flagging freight cost inflation and no concrete signs yet of adverse change to Section 232 tariffs from ongoing USMCA technical-level talks. On Brazil, management acknowledged import penetration remains structurally elevated and promised a more detailed competitiveness/restructuring plan in the following months, while pointing to the Miguel Burnier mining ramp as a near-term EBITDA driver independent of the steel price cycle.

bull_case: North America has become the dominant profit engine (~62% of 2025 consolidated EBITDA) and is structurally protected by 50% Section 232 tariffs, with demand upside from data centers, renewable energy and grid infrastructure build-out

Brazilian trade-defense measures (tariff-rate quotas through June 2027, anti-dumping duties) combined with eventual Selic rate cuts could drive a cyclical recovery in the currently depressed (~35% capacity utilization) domestic steel market

Low leverage (net debt/EBITDA ~0.69x) gives Gerdau flexibility to fund growth (Miguel Burnier mining expansion, Texas EAF expansion) while simultaneously returning capital via an active buyback (31% complete) and a minimum 30%-of-earnings dividend policy

Diversification across four business divisions and multiple countries reduces single-market dependence, and the mining/iron-ore self-sufficiency project adds a structural, less commodity-price-dependent EBITDA stream
Analyst sentiment has turned constructive, with price targets raised through 2026 (e.g., JP Morgan to $6.00, UBS to $5.25) reflecting improving North American fundamentals
bear_case: Group profitability is now highly dependent on U.S. Section 232 tariffs remaining at current (50%) levels; any easing via USMCA renegotiation or trade-policy reversal would directly compress North America's outsized EBITDA contribution

Brazilian operations remain structurally impaired by record import penetration (China supplying ~45% of LatAm imports, regional penetration ~40%) even with existing tariff protection, forcing costly restructuring (e.g., Açonorte/Recife) and casting doubt on the segment's medium-term earnings power

Steel remains a highly cyclical, commodity, price-taking business with essentially no customer switching costs or recurring revenue, making earnings volatile and difficult to forecast across the cycle

BRL currency volatility and sizeable unresolved Brazilian tax contingencies (billions of reais, some unreserved) add financial-statement and legal uncertainty not fully reflected in reported leverage metrics

Capital was pulled back from a ~$500 million Mexico special-steel investment due to tariff uncertainty, illustrating how quickly trade-policy shifts can impair Gerdau's growth capital allocation and strategic planning
